questions.q: How does the chapter define a citizen?
o: Someone who legally belongs to a country and is a member of its political community
Someone who has lived in a country for many years and thinks of it as home
Someone who was born in a country and has never lived in any other country
Someone who works in a country, earns there and pays taxes to its government
questions.a: A citizen is someone who legally belongs to a country and is a member of its political community, that is, someone who can take part in the decision-making of the country.

questions.q: Which of these statements about residents and citizens agrees with the chapter?
o: Not every resident of a country is a citizen of that country
Living in a country for many years makes a person its citizen
A citizen stops being a citizen once she lives in another country
A resident has the same formal, legal membership as a citizen
questions.a: Not every resident of a country is a citizen of it. Living in a place makes a person a resident, but citizenship is a formal, legal membership in a country; a citizen can even reside in another country.

questions.q:
Match each of the chapter's four concepts in Column I with the one-line meaning the chapter gives it in Column II.
Column I: 1. Rights  2. Duties  3. Discrimination  4. Inclusion
Column II: P. Unfair treatment based on identity  Q. Ensuring no one is left out because of language, religion, culture, ethnicity, caste or gender  R. Freedoms like equality, free speech, religion and education that let people live with dignity  S. Responsibilities such as obeying laws, paying taxes, keeping clean and helping others
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-R, 2-S, 3-P, 4-Q: rights are freedoms that let people live with dignity; duties are responsibilities such as obeying laws and paying taxes; discrimination is unfair treatment based on identity; inclusion ensures no one is left out.

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter names the Citizenship Act of 1955 and the Citizenship (Amendment) Act of 2019 as the laws that set the rules for gaining or losing citizenship in India.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the Citizenship Act of 1955 and the Citizenship (Amendment) Act of 2019 set the rules for gaining or losing citizenship; these laws deal with citizenship as a legal identity.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that these two Acts set the rules for gaining or losing citizenship (the legal side of citizenship)

questions.q: (a) Name two rights that the chapter says citizenship gives in a democracy. (b) Name two duties that it says citizens have.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: voting, free speech, and living and working safely. (b) Any two of: obeying the law, paying taxes, respecting others, and helping keep society safe.
s: (a) Names two rights: any two of voting, free speech, living and working safely
(b) Names two duties: any two of obeying the law, paying taxes, respecting others, helping keep society safe

questions.q: At a school book fair three children are left out. (i) Pooja is told she cannot read her poem on the stage because 'girls should stay behind the scenes'. (ii) Arjun, whose mother sweeps the streets, is stopped at the door of the reading corner while a rich trader's son walks straight in. (iii) Salim, who uses crutches, cannot reach the first-floor exhibition because the only way up is a long staircase. Name the ground on which each child is left out.
questions.a: (i) Pooja is left out because of her gender. (ii) Arjun is left out because of his economic background (his family is poor). (iii) Salim is left out because of his disability: there is no ramp or other way for him to reach the hall.
s: (i) Pooja: gender
(ii) Arjun: economic background
(iii) Salim: disability (no barrier-free way in)

questions.q:
Palm Grove Society in Kochi has 60 flats. In March its committee ran a two-part drive: families from 36 flats cleared plastic from the canal bank, families from 15 other flats taught evening classes to the children of construction workers, and families from the remaining 9 flats took no part. Mr Diego Alvarez, a citizen of Spain, has rented a flat there for five years and worked on the canal bank. At the next meeting the treasurer, an Indian citizen, says: 'I pay my taxes and I vote, so the society owes me a clean canal. Drives are for people with nothing better to do.'
(a) Using the chapter, is Mr Alvarez a resident of India, a citizen of India, or both? Give a reason.
(b) What percentage of the 60 flats took part in the drive?
(c) Which side of citizenship named in the chapter do the canal clean-up and the evening classes show?
(d) Using the chapter, judge the treasurer's view.
questions.a: (a) He is a resident but not a citizen of India: living in a place makes a person a resident, while citizenship is a formal, legal membership in a country, and not every resident is a citizen. (b) 36 + 15 = 51 flats took part; 51 of 60 = 85%. (c) Citizenship as a social responsibility: active participation such as helping others in need and protecting the environment. (d) Partly right, mostly not: paying taxes is a duty and voting is a right of citizenship, but the chapter says citizenship is about active participation, and its duties include not only paying taxes but also helping others in need and protecting the environment. As a social responsibility, citizenship unites people through shared values, rights and duties, so claiming a clean canal while refusing to help keep it clean does not fit the chapter's idea of a citizen.
s: (a) Resident but not citizen, because citizenship is a formal legal membership and not every resident is a citizen
(b) 51 of 60 flats = 85%
(c) Social responsibility: active participation such as helping others and protecting the environment
(d) Judges the view: taxes and voting count, but citizenship is active participation, including helping others and protecting the environment, and joins rights with duties

questions.q: According to the chapter, into how many broad categories does the Constitution group the Fundamental Rights?
o: Six
Five
Eleven
Four
questions.a: Six. The Constitution lists six broad categories of Fundamental Rights (Fig. 5.2). Eleven is the number of Fundamental Duties, and four is the number of concepts the chapter explores.

questions.q: The chapter's table of key articles lists 'Articles 29-30: Protection of language, script, and cultural rights; rights of minority institutions'. Ravi argues that a school run by a religious minority belongs under the right to freedom of religion, because the community is a religious one. Fig. 5.2 places the right to equality in Articles 14-18, the right to freedom of religion in Articles 25-28, cultural and educational rights in Articles 29 and 30, and the right to constitutional remedies in Article 32. Going by these article ranges, which category covers a minority community's right to run its own school?
o: Cultural and educational rights
Right to freedom of religion
Right to equality
Right to constitutional remedies
questions.a: Cultural and educational rights: the rights of minority institutions sit in Articles 29-30, which Fig. 5.2 names cultural and educational rights. The word 'religious' does not move it into the right to freedom of religion, which Fig. 5.2 limits to Articles 25-28.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Fundamental Rights can be enforced by law.
Reason (R): If Fundamental Rights are violated, people can approach the courts for justice.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says the rights can be enforced by law, which means that if they are violated people can approach the courts for justice.

questions.q: Name any four of the six broad categories of Fundamental Rights shown in Fig. 5.2.
questions.a: Any four of: the right to equality; the right to freedom; the right against exploitation; the right to freedom of religion; cultural and educational rights; the right to constitutional remedies.
s: Names two correct categories from Fig. 5.2
Names two more correct categories from Fig. 5.2

questions.q: For a class project, Ishaan drafts a model constitution with five categories of rights: equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights. To save space he leaves out the right to constitutional remedies. Using the chapter, give three reasons why his model protects citizens less well than the Indian Constitution does.
questions.a: (1) A citizen whose right is violated would have no right to approach the Supreme Court, which is what the right to constitutional remedies allows. (2) The other five categories would become promises on paper only, because nothing would ensure that they can actually be protected and enforced. (3) Since rights protect people from unfair actions by the government as well as by others, a citizen wronged by the government would have no sure way to stop that misuse of power. (Ambedkar called this right the very soul and heart of the Constitution, without which it would be a nullity.)
s: No way to approach the Supreme Court when a right is violated
The other rights become promises on paper that cannot be enforced
No sure protection against unfair action by the government or misuse of power (or Ambedkar's 'soul and heart' point, explained)

questions.q:
A legal-aid volunteer in a small town receives four requests in one week.
1. A grocer refuses to sell rice to Rekha because of her caste.
2. The municipal office turns Joseph down for a clerk's post only because of his religion.
3. A man wants help to claim 'a right to play loud music at 2 a.m.' next to a hospital.
4. A brick-factory owner makes adult workers work without fair wages and will not let them leave.
(a) Which request is not a right at all? Explain using the chapter's idea of rights as justified claims.
(b) Name the category of Fig. 5.2 that covers request 1 and request 2.
(c) Name the category of Fig. 5.2 that covers request 4.
(d) Which request is about unfair action by the government rather than by another person, and what does the chapter say rights do in such a case?
(e) If the rights in the other three requests are denied, where can the people turn, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Request 3. Rights are what people need to live with dignity, safety and respect; actions that cause harm to ourselves or others cannot be rights, and loud music at night beside a hospital harms the patients, so it is not a justified claim. (b) Right to equality: no one may be discriminated against because of caste or religion, and everyone has equal opportunity in jobs. (c) Right against exploitation: forcing people to work without fair wages is bonded labour, and the right makes it illegal to force anyone to work against their will. (d) Request 2, the municipal office. Fundamental rights protect people from unfair actions by the government as well as from unfair treatment by others, so that power is not misused. (e) They can approach the courts for justice; under the right to constitutional remedies citizens can approach the Supreme Court.
s: (a) Request 3, because an action that harms others is not a justified claim
(b) Right to equality for requests 1 and 2
(c) Right against exploitation for request 4 (bonded labour)
(d) Request 2; rights also protect people from unfair actions by the government
(e) The courts, including the Supreme Court under the right to constitutional remedies

questions.q:
At a legal-awareness camp in Bhilwara, volunteer Kavita pinned up six cards, one for each category of Fundamental Rights in Fig. 5.2, each with its article range. In one morning 48 visitors asked her questions: 20 asked about being treated equally when applying for jobs, 12 asked about being forced to work for no wages, 9 asked whether they could practise their own faith, and 7 asked what they could do if one of their rights was denied.
(a) Which card answers the largest group of visitors?
(b) Which card should Kavita point to for the 12 visitors who asked about forced work?
(c) Which card answers the 7 visitors, and what does that right allow them to do?
(d) Kavita tells everyone that these rights 'can be enforced by law'. What does the chapter say this means?
questions.a: (a) The right to equality (Articles 14-18), which covers equal opportunity in jobs; 20 of the 48 visitors asked about it. (b) The right against exploitation (Articles 23 and 24). (c) The right to constitutional remedies (Article 32): it allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court if their fundamental rights are violated. (d) If the rights are violated, people can approach the courts for justice.
s: (a) Right to equality, for the 20 questions on equal treatment in jobs
(b) Right against exploitation
(c) Right to constitutional remedies: approach the Supreme Court if a fundamental right is violated
(d) If the rights are violated, people can approach the courts for justice

questions.q: In Fig. 5.3 of the chapter, what does the panel labelled EQUALITY show?
o: Everyone receives the exact same support
Everyone gets the support they need, fairly
The barrier is taken away so that no support is needed
Those who were held back receive all of the support
questions.a: The EQUALITY panel shows everyone receiving the exact same support. 'Everyone gets the support they need, fairly' is the EQUITY panel.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the right to equality and Fig. 5.3.
I. The right to equality gives equal opportunities in education as well as in jobs.
II. Under the right to equality, the government may not give a special title to anyone, not even for a military honour.
III. Fig. 5.3 shows that giving everyone the same support always gives everyone the same benefit.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong because the bar on special titles has an exception for military and academic honours. Statement III is wrong because the chapter says providing the same thing to everyone does not always give the same benefit, because of differences among people.

questions.q: (a) Give the chapter's definition of equity. (b) Name the campaign the chapter gives as an example of an initiative to establish equity.
questions.a: (a) Equity is the quality of being fair and just, especially in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing inequalities. (b) The Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaign, which built awareness in society and provided support to girls' education.
s: (a) Equity: being fair and just in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing inequalities
(b) Beti Bachao Beti Padhao

questions.q: During a heatwave, a municipal ward sends a tanker that gives every household the same 20 litres of drinking water a day, whether the household has 2 members or 9. (a) Which panel of Fig. 5.3 does this plan follow? (b) Using the chapter, explain why this plan may not give every household the same benefit, and suggest one change that would follow the other panel.
questions.a: (a) Equality: every household receives the exact same support. (b) The chapter says that giving the same thing to everyone does not always give the same benefit, because of differences among them; 20 litres goes much further for 2 people than for 9. Following equity, each household could be given water according to its need, for example a fixed amount per member.
s: (a) Equality: the exact same support for every household
(b) Same support does not give the same benefit because of differences among people, with an equity change such as water according to the number of members

questions.q: State three things that the right to equality guarantees, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Any three of: every person is treated equally before the law; equal opportunities in jobs and education; no one can be discriminated against because of religion, race, caste, gender or place of birth; an end to practices like untouchability; the government may not give special titles to individuals, except for military or academic honours.
s: First correct guarantee (for example, equality before the law)
Second correct guarantee (for example, equal opportunity in jobs and education)
Third correct guarantee (for example, the end of untouchability, no discrimination on the five grounds, or no special titles except military or academic honours)

questions.q: Answer these four short parts on equality and equity. (a) State what equality means in Fig. 5.3. (b) State what equity means in Fig. 5.3. (c) Give the chapter's reason why providing the same thing to every individual does not always provide the same benefit. (d) A district gives free bus passes only to girls from villages that have no secondary school, so that they can reach a school in the next town. Is this equality or equity? Give one reason.
questions.a: (a) Everyone receives the exact same support. (b) Everyone gets the support they need, fairly. (c) Because of differences among people, which can be due to inequality and discrimination, sometimes carried from the past. (d) Equity: the passes go only to the girls who face a barrier the others do not, giving them the support they need instead of giving everyone the same thing.
s: (a) Equality: everyone receives the exact same support
(b) Equity: everyone gets the support they need, fairly
(c) Differences among people, which can come from inequality and discrimination carried historically
(d) Equity, because support goes to those who need it to overcome a gap

questions.q:
A school of 200 students announces a science olympiad. The only way to enter is an online form. 160 students have internet at home and 40 do not. 64 of the 160 students with internet enter, but only 2 of the 40 without internet do. The headmaster says, 'The same form was open to all, so we have been perfectly fair.'
(a) Which principle in Fig. 5.3 is the school following?
(b) Work out the percentage of students who entered in each group.
(c) Using the chapter, explain why the same support did not give the same benefit.
(d) Suggest one step that would follow the principle of equity.
(e) A parent of one of the 160 says equity would be unfair to her child. Reply using the chapter's definition of equity.
questions.a: (a) Equality: everyone received the exact same support, one online form. (b) 64 of 160 is 40%; 2 of 40 is 5%. (c) The chapter says giving the same thing to everyone does not always give the same benefit because of differences among people, which can be due to inequality; here the difference is access to the internet. (d) For example, paper forms or entry through the school computer room during school hours for the 40 students without internet. (e) Equity means being fair and just in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing inequalities; it gives the 40 the support they need to reach the same starting point, and her child still keeps the same chance to enter.
s: (a) Equality: the same support for all
(b) 40% of the students with internet and 5% of those without
(c) Same support, different benefit, because of differences such as access to the internet
(d) A sensible equity step such as paper forms or school computer access for the 40
(e) Equity addresses existing inequalities, and the other students lose nothing

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does the right to freedom allow people to do?
o: Express themselves, move freely, and choose how they live and work
Do anything they like, with no limits of any kind, as long as they believe it is right
Set up and manage schools that teach in their own community's language
Approach the Supreme Court whenever one of their rights is violated
questions.a: The right to freedom allows people to express themselves, move freely, and choose how they want to live and work, within reasonable restrictions.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In New Zealand, the Whanganui River is legally treated as a living being.
Reason (R): In India too, the Ganga and the Yamuna still hold the rights of a living person under the 2017 order of the Uttarakhand High Court.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The chapter says the Whanganui River is legally treated as a living being, but the 2017 Uttarakhand High Court decision on the Ganga and Yamuna was suspended and finally overturned by the Supreme Court, which called it legally unsustainable.

questions.q: True or False? 'The right to life, as the chapter describes it, includes the right to health but not the right to education.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the right to life means living with dignity, and it includes the right to livelihood, education, health, a clean environment and fair treatment under the law; so education is included as well as health.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the right to life includes livelihood, education, health, a clean environment and fair treatment under the law

questions.q: A forest fire breaks out near a hill town, and the district closes the only road up the hill to tourists for three days. A tourist complains that this breaks his right to freedom. (a) Which freedom named in the chapter is being limited? (b) Using the chapter's idea of reasonable restrictions, say whether the closure can be justified.
questions.a: (a) The freedom to move freely. (b) Yes. The chapter says freedoms are not unlimited; they come with reasonable restrictions so that they are not misused or harmful to others or the nation. Letting tourists drive towards a fire could harm them and others, so a short closure is a reasonable restriction.
s: (a) Freedom to move freely
(b) Justified, because freedoms carry reasonable restrictions so that they do not harm others

questions.q: Arjun says: 'The right to freedom and the right to life are really the same right, because both simply let a person do whatever she wants.' Test his claim against the chapter. Give your verdict, then explain what each right actually covers.
questions.a: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong. The right to freedom lets people express themselves, move freely and choose how to live and work, but these freedoms come with reasonable restrictions, so it is not 'whatever she wants'. The right to life protects a person's life and liberty and means living with dignity: it includes livelihood, education, health, a clean environment and fair treatment under the law, and protects children with disabilities. It is about the conditions for a dignified life, not about doing what one wants.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Right to freedom: expression, movement, choice of how to live and work, with reasonable restrictions
Right to life: life and liberty with dignity, including livelihood, education, health, clean environment and fair treatment

questions.q:
For each situation, name the part of the right to life, as the chapter lists it, that is at stake.
(a) A family loses the small shop that was its only source of income.
(b) A girl is kept at home and not allowed to attend school.
(c) A government clinic turns away a sick child.
(d) A town dumps its garbage into the lake that people live around.
(e) A man is punished without being given a chance to be heard.
questions.a: (a) The right to livelihood. (b) The right to education. (c) The right to health. (d) The right to a clean environment. (e) Fair treatment under the law.
s: (a) Livelihood
(b) Education
(c) Health
(d) A clean environment
(e) Fair treatment under the law

questions.q:
In April, the student council of a school with 640 students asked the principal to let students wear light sports clothes for outdoor PT during the hot months. The council ran a survey: 480 students supported the change, saying comfort and safety matter while playing; 160 opposed it, saying the uniform shows discipline and equality among students. During the same week, someone stuck anonymous posters on the school walls calling the principal 'cruel'.
(a) Which freedom were the council members using when they put their request to the principal?
(b) What percentage of the students supported the change?
(c) Using the chapter's idea of reasonable restrictions, explain why the school may act against the posters while still welcoming the survey.
(d) Should the principal allow sports clothes for PT? Give a decision that weighs both groups of students and the school's rules.
questions.a: (a) Freedom of speech and expression. (b) 480 of 640 = 75%. (c) Freedoms are not unlimited: they come with reasonable restrictions so that they are not misused or harmful to others. The survey raised a concern in a fair way, while the anonymous posters insult a person and deface the walls, which misuses the freedom. (d) A reasoned decision, for example: allow sports clothes and shoes only on PT and Sports Days, since three quarters asked for it on grounds of comfort and safety, while keeping the full uniform on other days to respect the minority's point about discipline and equality; the change is made through the school's rules, not by ignoring them.
s: (a) Freedom of speech and expression
(c) Reasonable restrictions stop a freedom being misused or harmful to others; the posters misuse it, the survey does not
(d) A decision that weighs the 75% (comfort, safety) against the 25% (discipline, equality) and works through the school's rules

questions.q: How did the children's helpline Childline 1098 begin, according to the chapter?
o: As an action project at an educational institution in the late 1990s
As an order of the Supreme Court after the 2015 factory rescue
As one of the Fundamental Duties added to the Constitution in 2002
As a helpline set up by factory owners to report their own workers
questions.a: It started as an action project at an educational institution in the late 1990s and soon became a national-level helpline.

questions.q: Twelve-year-old Ravi helps at his family's small shop that sells clay pots, during his summer vacation. Which ONE change would make this break the chapter's rule on employing children below 14?
o: He is sent instead to work at a stone mine near the village
He also helps at the shop for an hour each evening after school
He also helps at the shop during the winter vacation
His fifteen-year-old sister also starts helping at the shop
questions.a: Being sent to work at a mine breaks the rule, because there is a ban on work in places such as factories, mines and restaurants. Helping in a non-hazardous family enterprise during vacations or after school hours is allowed.

questions.q:
Match each child in Column I with the verdict in Column II that the chapter's account of exploitation and its rule on children below 14 would give.
Column I: 1. A twelve-year-old works full time washing dishes in a restaurant  2. A thirteen-year-old helps in his family's non-hazardous handloom shop after school hours  3. A ten-year-old is kept from school to help in her family's non-hazardous shop during school hours  4. A nine-year-old is sold by an agent to work in another city
Column II: P. Not allowed: work in such a place is banned  Q. Allowed: help in a non-hazardous family enterprise outside school hours  R. Not allowed: family help is permitted only during vacations or after school hours  S. Human trafficking: being traded or sold for profit
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-P, 2-Q, 3-R, 4-S: restaurants are named among the banned workplaces; family help in a non-hazardous enterprise after school is allowed; help during school hours breaks the timing condition; selling a child for profit is human trafficking.

questions.q: Name any two forms of exploitation that the chapter lists, and give the meaning the chapter attaches to each.
questions.a: Any two of: bonded labour, when people are forced to work without fair wages; human trafficking, when people are traded or sold for profit; the abuse or unfair treatment of women or children; child labour, when children are made to work instead of going to school, particularly in hazardous situations.
s: First form named with its meaning (for example, bonded labour: forced to work without fair wages)
Second form named with its meaning (for example, human trafficking: traded or sold for profit)

questions.q: Recount the 2015 Childline 1098 rescue described in the chapter. (a) How did the helpline learn about the children? (b) What did the team find when it visited? (c) What happened after the visit?
questions.a: (a) A concerned citizen called Childline 1098 about 20 children being forced to work in a factory that embroidered clothes. (b) The children were being forced to work in a congested, unhealthy room and got food only once a day, which was not nourishing. (c) The team rescued the children, gave them medical care and ensured they would be taken care of, and the culprits were arrested.
s: (a) A call from a concerned citizen about 20 children forced to work in an embroidery factory
(b) Forced work in a congested, unhealthy room with one non-nourishing meal a day
(c) Children rescued and given medical care and future care; culprits arrested

questions.q: A district survey of 500 children aged 6 to 13 finds that 415 go to school and do no work; 40 help in their family's non-hazardous shops after school or in vacations; 30 work in roadside restaurants during school hours; and 15 work in a stone mine. The district team can run only one inspection drive this month. (a) Which of the four groups does the chapter's rule allow, and which does it forbid? (b) How many children, and what percentage of the 500, are in forbidden work? (c) Should the team go first to the restaurants or to the mine? Justify using the chapter. (d) Suggest one thing an ordinary citizen could do about the children still left.
questions.a: (a) The 415 at school and the 40 helping in non-hazardous family enterprises outside school hours are within the rule; the 30 in restaurants and the 15 in the mine are in forbidden work, since the chapter bans work in places such as factories, mines and restaurants. (b) 30 + 15 = 45 children, which is 9% of 500. (c) A justified choice: the mine, because the chapter stresses child labour particularly in hazardous situations and children's safety; or the restaurants, because they hold twice as many children (30 against 15), who are all missing school. Either is accepted if the trade-off is stated. (d) For example, call Childline 1098, or tell a teacher or the principal, as the chapter suggests.
s: (a) Allowed: the 415 and the 40; forbidden: the 30 in restaurants and the 15 in the mine
(b) 45 children, 9%
(c) A decision weighing the greater danger at the mine against the larger number in restaurants
(d) A step such as calling Childline 1098 or telling a teacher

questions.q:
A Childline 1098 team, acting on a call from a bus conductor, stops a bus at a highway town. Two agents are travelling with 24 children aged 9 to 13. The agents had paid each child's family Rs 2,000 and promised 'good work in a big city'. Their notebook shows that 16 children were to be handed over to a bangle factory, 5 to restaurant kitchens, and 3 were to work all day as house helpers in the agents' own homes. None of the 24 has been to school this year.
(a) Which form of exploitation named in the chapter are the agents carrying out?
(b) What percentage of the 24 children were bound for kinds of workplace that the chapter names as banned for children below 14?
(c) The agents say the 3 house helpers are fine because a home is not a factory. Does the chapter's rule on children below 14 allow their work? Give the reason.
(d) The agents also say, 'The families agreed and took the money, so no one is being forced.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Human trafficking: the children are being traded or sold for profit. (b) The factory and the restaurants are named among the banned workplaces: 16 + 5 = 21 children, and 21 of 24 = 87.5%. (c) No. In general children below 14 may not be employed; the only exception is helping in a non-hazardous family enterprise, and only during vacations or after school hours. Working all day in the agents' homes is neither family help nor outside school hours, and it keeps them out of school. (d) The claim fails. The right against exploitation makes it illegal to force anyone to work against their will, and children need special protection because they depend on adults, may not understand their rights and cannot stand up for themselves; money paid to a family does not make selling a child for work acceptable. The children are also losing education, play and a healthy childhood.
s: (a) Human trafficking: being traded or sold for profit
(b) 21 of 24 = 87.5% (factory and restaurants are banned workplaces)
(c) Not allowed: only help in a non-hazardous family enterprise in vacations or after school hours is permitted; this is neither
(d) Rejects the claim: forced work is illegal and children need special protection since they depend on adults and cannot stand up for themselves; payment to the family changes nothing

questions.q: According to the chapter, what are state-run or government-aided schools NOT allowed to do?
o: Promote any particular religion
Admit students who follow different religions
Teach students in their regional language
Celebrate India's cultural diversity in assemblies
questions.a: They are not allowed to promote any particular religion. This helps protect India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state.

questions.q:
Read the statements about cultural and educational rights.
I. No student can be denied admission to a government institution because of religion, caste, race or language.
II. Cultural and educational rights let a community preserve its script, but not its traditions.
III. These rights help maintain cultural identity while supporting equality and non-discrimination.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the chapter says communities can preserve their language, script and traditions.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): State-run or government-aided schools in India are not allowed to promote any particular religion.
Reason (R): Religious and linguistic minorities have the right to set up and manage their own schools.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The chapter's reason for A is that it protects India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state; R is a separate cultural and educational right about minority schools.

questions.q: Mr Fernandes hands out leaflets about his faith in a market, peacefully, to anyone who wishes to take one. The owner of a garment unit makes all his workers attend the prayers of his own religion every morning or lose a day's wages. (a) Which of the two is using the right to freedom of religion as the chapter describes it? (b) Which part of that right does the other person break?
questions.a: (a) Mr Fernandes: the right lets every person choose, practise and share their religion freely. (b) The garment-unit owner breaks the part that ensures no one is forced to follow a particular religion.
s: (a) Mr Fernandes, who is sharing his religion freely
(b) The owner breaks the rule that no one may be forced to follow a particular religion

questions.q: Compare the right to freedom of religion with cultural and educational rights. (a) State one thing the right to freedom of religion protects. (b) State one thing cultural and educational rights protect. (c) Explain one way the two rights work together for a diverse country like India.
questions.a: (a) Every person may choose, practise and share their religion freely, and no one may be forced to follow, propagate or fund a particular religion. (b) Communities can preserve their language, script and traditions; no student can be denied admission to a government institution because of religion, caste, race or language; minorities may set up and manage their own schools. (c) Together they safeguard cultural identity while promoting equal access to education and keeping all faiths equal in the eyes of the state, which protects India's diversity.
s: (a) One protection of the right to freedom of religion
(b) One protection of cultural and educational rights
(c) They work together: cultural identity is kept while equality, equal access and equal treatment of faiths are upheld

questions.q:
A district education office receives four complaints in one month.
1. A state-run school makes every student recite the prayers of one religion at the morning assembly.
2. A government college refuses a student admission only because of her caste.
3. A Gujarati-speaking minority community runs its own school, and a neighbour says the school is illegal.
4. A housing society tells new families they must pay towards building a place of worship of one religion before they are given a flat.
(a) Complaint 1, (b) Complaint 2, (c) Complaint 3, (d) Complaint 4: for each, say whether a right is broken and name the right from the chapter that applies.
(e) Which complaint touches the tension the chapter describes between protecting minorities and upholding equality? Explain the tension.
questions.a: (a) Complaint 1: yes; state-run schools may not promote any particular religion (right to freedom of religion). (b) Complaint 2: yes; no student can be denied admission to a government institution because of caste (cultural and educational rights). The right to equality, which gives equal opportunities in education and forbids discrimination because of caste, is also accepted. (c) Complaint 3: no right is broken; religious and linguistic minorities have the right to set up and manage their own schools (cultural and educational rights). (d) Complaint 4: yes; no one may be forced to fund a particular religion (right to freedom of religion). (e) Complaint 3. The Constitution protects the rights of minorities, while also upholding equality and non-discrimination on the basis of religion; at times these aims can seem to be in conflict, and some people feel minority protections may go against the idea of secularism.
s: (a) Complaint 1 breaks freedom of religion: state-run schools may not promote a religion

(b) Complaint 2 breaks a right: cultural and educational rights (no denial of admission on caste) or the right to equality (equal opportunity in education, no caste discrimination); either is accepted
(c) Complaint 3 breaks no right: minorities may run their own schools
(d) Complaint 4 breaks freedom of religion: no one may be forced to fund a religion
(e) Complaint 3, with the tension between minority protection and equality or non-discrimination explained

questions.q: In which year were Fundamental Duties added to the Indian Constitution, according to the chapter?
questions.a: 1976. The Constitution had no Fundamental Duties when it came into effect in 1950; they were added in 1976 by an amendment, and the 11th duty followed in 2002.

questions.q: Kavya hears a rumour that food cooked during a solar eclipse turns poisonous. Before believing it, she reads about eclipses and asks her science teacher for evidence. Which Fundamental Duty is she following?
o: Develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry
Strive for excellence in all the activities she takes up
Preserve the culture and heritage of her town and country
Follow the noble ideals of India's freedom struggle
questions.a: She is developing scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry, by checking a claim against evidence instead of simply believing it.

questions.q:
Match each idea in Column I with the situation in Column II that fits the way the chapter explains it.
Column I: 1. Dharma  2. Rina  3. Adhikara (in ancient texts)  4. A Fundamental Duty
Column II: P. Only a person trained and competent in healing is given the right to treat the sick  Q. Meera feels she owes care to her parents, her teachers and Nature simply because she was born  R. A villager acts for what is beneficial to people and to society, which goes beyond a narrow sense of duty  S. A citizen stands for the National Anthem, as Article 51A asks
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-R, 2-Q, 3-P, 4-S: dharma has a wide meaning including what is beneficial to people and society; rina is the debt owed to devatas, ancestors and parents, gurus, fellow humans and Nature by being born; adhikara in ancient texts meant capacity, competence or authority; respecting the National Anthem is the first duty in Article 51A.

questions.q: (a) When Fundamental Duties were first added, how many were there, and in which Article were they listed? (b) What does the 11th duty, added in 2002, require?
questions.a: (a) There were 10 duties, listed in Article 51A (Part IV-A). (b) Parents or guardians must make sure that children between 6 and 14 years of age get an education.
s: (a) 10 duties in Article 51A (Part IV-A)
(b) Parents or guardians must ensure education for children aged 6 to 14

questions.q: True or False? 'Fundamental Duties are only for adults, since they are about things like defending the nation and helping in emergencies; a school student has no Fundamental Duty to perform.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says duties are the responsibility each one of us has towards our family, community, country and environment, and most of its examples of the Fundamental Duties are from school life: students standing silently for the National Anthem, a student stopping a friend from writing on a fort wall (preserving heritage), and students stopping a group from teasing a girl (respecting women).
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: duties are everyone's responsibility, with a school-life example of a Fundamental Duty from the chapter

questions.q: Read the three situations and answer the parts. Situation 1: After a festival, some young men spray-paint their names on a new bus shelter. Situation 2: An eleven-year-old boy has been taken out of school by his father to look after the family's tea stall all day. Situation 3: Students put up a sign at a centuries-old step-well in their town asking visitors not to scratch their names on its carved walls. (a)-(c) Name the Fundamental Duty involved in each situation. (d) The chapter calls duties moral and social responsibilities. Using Situation 1, explain how this differs from the way rights are protected.
questions.a: (a) Situation 1: protect public property and avoid violence. (b) Situation 2: ensure education for children aged 6 to 14, the duty of parents or guardians. (c) Situation 3: preserve culture and heritage. (d) Rights are protected by law, and a person whose rights are violated, even by the government, can go to court. Duties are moral and social responsibilities that we are expected to follow, but not doing so may not always lead to legal action; so in Situation 1 the young men have failed a duty to the community even if no case is filed.
s: (a) Situation 1: protect public property and avoid violence
(b) Situation 2: ensure education for children aged 6 to 14
(c) Situation 3: preserve culture and heritage
(d) Rights are protected by law and can be taken to court; duties are moral and social responsibilities whose neglect may not always lead to legal action

questions.q:
On Independence Day the residents of Shanti Nagar in Nagpur held a 'Duty Day'. 25 children picked up plastic from the playground and planted saplings, 12 adults repaired the broken benches of the public park instead of leaving them to rot, 8 teenagers set out bowls of water for stray dogs, and 5 senior citizens took the children around the town's old stone gate and told them its history.
(a) Which Fundamental Duty did the 12 adults carry out?
(b) Which Fundamental Duty did the 5 senior citizens carry out?
(c) The work of the 25 children and the 8 teenagers falls under one Fundamental Duty. Name it.
(d) How many people took part in all, and what percentage of them worked on the park benches?
questions.a: (a) Protect public property and avoid violence. (b) Preserve culture and heritage. (c) Protect and improve the environment and have compassion towards animals. (d) 25 + 12 + 8 + 5 = 50 people; 12 of 50 is 24%.
s: (a) Protect public property
(b) Preserve culture and heritage
(c) Protect and improve the environment and have compassion towards animals
(d) 50 people in all; 24% worked on the benches

questions.q: According to the chapter, what did Savitribai Phule establish in the mid-19th century?
o: A school for girls
A medical college for women
A helpline for working children
A reading club for regional languages
questions.a: She established a school for girls, at a time when people believed girls should not go to school, and remained steadfast though she was abused and had mud thrown at her.

questions.q: A residents' group never invites one family to its festival celebrations because of the family's caste, though nobody says a word about it openly. When the family complains, the committee asks them to show proof. Which point in the chapter does this case illustrate?
o: Invisible discrimination is difficult to prove, and so difficult to penalise
Discrimination is unethical but is not prohibited by law
Only open insults count as discrimination under the Constitution
Discrimination harms the person but has no effect on society
questions.a: Invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and hence difficult to penalise. Leaving someone out of a celebration because of their social background is indirect discrimination.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): According to the chapter, a person who discriminates against others still remains, ethically, an active citizen of India.
Reason (R): The chapter calls respect and unity the very core of the Indian Constitution.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. The chapter says a person who discriminates ethically ceases to be an active citizen, because they have breached the very core of the Constitution, that is, respect and unity.

questions.q: About Anandibai Joshi, as the chapter tells her story: (a) Why did she decide to study medicine? (b) Where did she go to study?
questions.a: (a) Her baby died soon after birth because of lack of medical care, and she decided to become a doctor so that she could serve mothers and children. (b) The Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania.
s: (a) Her baby died for lack of medical care; she wanted to serve mothers and children
(b) The Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania

questions.q: Name the ground of discrimination, from the chapter's list, in each case. (i) A guest house refuses a room to a family because of the religion they follow. (ii) A sports club turns away a girl who is visually impaired. (iii) Classmates refuse to sit with a boy because he is very short.
questions.a: (i) Religion. (ii) Disability. (iii) Physical appearance.
s: (i) Religion
(ii) Disability
(iii) Physical appearance

questions.q:
Three things happen at a coaching centre. (i) The receptionist tells Shabnam, whose father is a daily-wage labourer, that the 'top batch is not for people like her'. (ii) When students form project groups, nobody ever picks Raju, who wears a hearing aid; no one says anything unkind, he is simply never chosen. (iii) A teacher keeps making jokes about the cap that Imtiaz wears for his religion.
(a) Name the ground of discrimination in each case.
(b) Which case is the clearest example of invisible discrimination? Give the reason.
(c) Why does the chapter say invisible discrimination is a major problem?
(d) State two effects the chapter says discrimination has.
(e) Suggest one deliberate action the centre could take, and link it to the chapter's closing points.
questions.a: (a) (i) Economic background; (ii) disability; (iii) religion. (b) Case (ii): Raju is excluded, or nobody is willing to include him in a project, without any open act, which is indirect discrimination. (c) Invisible discrimination is difficult to prove, and hence difficult to penalise. (d) Any two of: it affects the person psychologically and physically; it affects society as a whole; it creates a social barrier that hampers people from enjoying their fundamental rights. (e) For example, teachers form mixed project groups and set a rule against jokes about anyone's religion; the chapter says deliberate actions need to be taken to prevent discrimination and ensure inclusion.
s: (a) Economic background, disability and religion
(b) Case (ii), because he is quietly excluded without any open act
(c) It is difficult to prove and therefore difficult to penalise
(d) Two effects: harm to the person (psychological and physical), harm to society, or a barrier to fundamental rights
(e) A deliberate action linked to the chapter's point that deliberate actions are needed to prevent discrimination

questions.q: How does the chapter explain the meaning of inclusion?
o: Creating an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected, valued and included, with equal access to opportunities
Giving every person exactly the same support and the same facilities, whatever their needs or background
Giving each person the support they need, fairly, so that past inequalities between groups are addressed
Reserving a share of seats in schools and jobs for groups that have been excluded in the past
questions.a: Inclusion means creating an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected, valued and included, with equal access to opportunities. The other options describe equality, equity and reservations; the chapter says inclusion goes beyond just giving reservations.

questions.q:
Read the statements about inclusion.
I. Inclusion can mean finding ways for people who speak different languages to communicate.
II. A class invites every student, including Tara, who uses crutches, to a picnic at a hilltop reached only by a steep path; since no one was left off the invitation list, this fits the chapter's idea of inclusion.
III. In the chapter's account, fundamental rights support inclusion, but fundamental duties have no part in it.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong: inclusion also means equal access and removing barriers to participation, and the steep path keeps Tara from taking part even though she was invited. Statement III is wrong: the chapter says that in the Constitution fundamental rights and duties together support inclusion.

questions.q: Give two practical examples of inclusion that the chapter names.
questions.a: Any two of: finding ways for people speaking different languages to communicate; welcoming students from all castes, religions or backgrounds into schools; giving extra help such as braille books, ramps or classroom support to children with special needs; removing barriers to participation.
s: First practical example from the chapter
Second practical example from the chapter

questions.q: The school library is on the first floor, reached only by stairs, and Neha uses a wheelchair. The school considers three plans. Plan 1: every student, Neha included, gets the same 30 minutes of library time each week. Plan 2: a helper brings down any books Neha asks for. Plan 3: the library moves to the ground floor with a ramp at its door, so Neha can go in and choose books like everyone else. Each plan best matches a different one of the chapter's ideas of equality, equity and inclusion. Say which idea each plan matches best, with a reason.
questions.a: Plan 1 matches equality: everyone receives the exact same support, but Neha still cannot reach the library. Plan 2 matches equity: she is given the support she needs, but the barrier (the stairs) stays and she still cannot choose books like the others. Plan 3 matches inclusion: it removes the barrier to participation, so she has equal access and takes part like everyone else.
s: Plan 1: equality, the same support for all, though Neha still cannot reach it
Plan 2: equity, the support she needs, while the barrier remains
Plan 3: inclusion, the barrier to participation is removed

questions.q:
A school of 700 students holds its annual science exhibition in a first-floor hall reached only by stairs. 35 of its students have special needs: 15 use wheelchairs or crutches, 12 are visually impaired and 8 need classroom support. Last year only 7 of these 35 students showed a project. The exhibition budget is Rs 48,000. Plan A: hold a separate ground-floor 'special exhibition' for the 35 students on another day, costing Rs 12,000 and leaving Rs 36,000 for materials and prizes. Plan B: move the main exhibition to the ground floor with a ramp, add braille labels to the exhibits and give helpers to the students who need classroom support, costing Rs 30,000 and leaving Rs 18,000 for materials and prizes.
(a) What percentage of the school's students have special needs?
(b) What percentage of these 35 students showed a project last year, and how many were left out?
(c) Using the chapter's definition of inclusion, compare what Plan A and Plan B do.
(d) Which plan would you advise? Justify your choice, using the chapter's idea of removing barriers to participation and its closing point about democracy.
questions.a: (a) 35 of 700 = 5%. (b) 7 of 35 = 20% showed a project, so 35 - 7 = 28 students were left out. (c) Inclusion means an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected, valued and included, with equal access to opportunities. Plan A gives the 35 students a chance to show projects but keeps them apart from the main exhibition; Plan B brings them into the same exhibition and removes the barriers (stairs, print-only labels, no support), using the kinds of extra help the chapter names: ramps, braille and classroom support. (d) Plan B is better supported by the chapter: inclusion means removing barriers to participation, and democracy is strengthened by enabling and facilitating the participation of all, which matters when 28 of 35 were left out last year. The cost is half the money for materials and prizes (Rs 18,000 instead of Rs 36,000), which the answer should weigh; a student may also argue for phasing part of Plan B, if reasoned.
s: (b) 20%; 28 students left out
(c) Plan A separates the 35 students; Plan B includes them in the same exhibition and removes barriers, related to the definition of inclusion
(d) A justified choice that weighs the smaller prize money against removing barriers to participation and enabling the participation of all

questions.q:
The Ward 7 community library in Mysuru has 1,200 members. To find out why others never come, volunteers surveyed 300 adults living nearby who are not members. 120 said almost all the books are in English, 90 said they cannot climb the twelve steps at the entrance (most of them elderly people or wheelchair users), 60 said the library is open only from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., when they are at work, and 30 gave other reasons. This year the library can afford only one change.
(a) What percentage of the people surveyed named the language of the books?
(b) Two of these barriers match practical examples of inclusion that the chapter gives. Name them and the chapter's examples.
(c) The library is already open to anyone who wants to join. Using the chapter's own words, what more does inclusion ask for?
(d) Which one change should the library make first? Justify using the survey data and the chapter's closing points.
questions.a: (a) 120 of 300 = 40%. (b) The language barrier matches 'finding ways for people speaking different languages to communicate' (as Smt. Amita's club did with regional-language books); the steps match giving extra help such as ramps. (c) Inclusion means creating an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected, valued and included, with equal access to opportunities; it also means removing barriers to participation. (d) A justified choice: regional-language books reach the largest group (40%); a ramp removes a barrier that keeps 90 people (30%) out completely, whatever books are there. Either is accepted if it uses the data and the chapter's points that deliberate actions are needed to ensure inclusion and that democracy is strengthened through enabling the participation of all.
s: (b) Language (different languages communicating) and steps (ramps)
(c) Inclusion is feeling welcomed and valued with equal access, and removing barriers to participation
(d) A decision that weighs the larger language group against the complete barrier of the steps, linked to the chapter's closing points
